newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech NATO membership could cost $200 mln a year.
newsitem.headline: Czech NATO membership could cost $200 mln a year.

text.p: Modernising the Czech armed forces to prepare them for NATO membership could cost the country an extra $200 million a year, a leading Czech politician said on Tuesday.

Speaking at a conference to mark the 52nd anniversary of the liberation of Plzen by U.S. forces, Civic Democratic Alliance party leader Michael Zantovsky said the Czechs had between 18 months and two years to prepare for membership.

"I cannot imagine how, considering the current level of financing of our armed forces, we can manage to be ready within this fairly short period of time," Zantovsky, a former Czech ambassador to Washington, told the conference.
"I believe more attention will have to be paid to this question and also more money will have to be allocated to pursue this objective," he added.
Asked later about the likely extra cost, Zantovsky said: "The figures I have seen would represent something between $100 million and $200 million a year."
However he said the cost of joining NATO would work out less than other security arrangements, such as staying neutral.

The Czech Republic, along with Poland and Hungary, is a leading contender to be among the first wave of new members of the North Atlantic Treaty Orgainsation (NATO). The alliance is due to issue invitations to join after a July summit in Madrid.
Zantovsky said that with Czech membership requiring ratification by all NATO states' parliaments, Prague would have to prove to alliance members that it would make a contribution and not be a burden.
"It would be foolish to assume that this ratification can be taken for granted once the decision in Madrid is taken."

Zantovsky, whose party is a member of the ruling coalition but who is not himself in the government, said the air force would need modernising and the army reorganising to be compatible with NATO forces.

Opinion polls show Czechs lukewarm so far to the idea of joining a military alliance. The former Czechoslovakia, which split peacefully into the Czech and Slovak republics in 1993, was a member of the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact.
In August 1968, Warsaw Pact forces invaded Czechoslovakia to crush the brief "Prague Spring" attempt to introduce "socialism with a human face".
Czech leaders often stress that NATO membership would mean joining a group of like-minded states rather than an overtly mililtary grouping.
U.S. ambassador to Prague Jenonne Walker told the conference that NATO would always primarily be a military alliance but cautioned against the cost of staying out.
"Going it alone is much more expensive than collective defence," she said.
